title: How to get rid of old furniture: donate, sell, or haul
summary: Sell or donate the good pieces. For damaged furniture, use bulk pickup, recycle it, or book Lugg to carry it to the destination you choose.
body_markdown:
The best way to get rid of old furniture depends on three things: its condition, your deadline, and whether someone can carry and transport it. Sell a clean piece with real resale value, give away or donate usable furniture, and use city bulk pickup, a recycling center, or a dump for anything damaged or worn out. At Lugg over the past year, a donation drop-off cost a median of about $120 before tip, while a haul to the dump cost a median of about $185 before tip.


You don't have to own or rent a truck when the piece needs to leave the building. Lugg is an on-demand moving and delivery service that carries old furniture from your home to the buyer, donation center, dump, or recycling center you choose. It's built for the sofa that won't fit in your car or the dresser you can't get down three flights of stairs alone, with movers on the way within the hour or in a one-hour window you pick.


The table below compares each furniture-disposal route by the condition it fits, what it requires from you, and typical timing.


Route Use it when Who handles the carry and transport Typical timing


Sell it The piece is clean and has real resale value The buyer, unless delivery is arranged Days to weeks


Give it away The piece is usable, but speed matters more than price The taker, if the listing says pickup Often a day or two


Donate it The piece is clean, complete, and working You, a charity pickup, or movers you book Depends on the charity


City bulk pickup The piece is damaged or worn out and local rules allow it You get it to the curb unless the city says otherwise The next collection date


Haul it to a dump or recycler The piece is unusable and has to go on a deadline You or movers you book Same day when available


## How should you get rid of old furniture?


Choose how to get rid of old furniture by checking its condition first. Ask whether you'd buy the piece from a stranger at a third of what you paid. A stained mattress, a cracked frame, pet damage, or a smoke smell ends the sale and the donation in one go, so a piece like that skips straight to bulk pickup or the dump. A solid wood dresser with a scratched top is the opposite case: someone wants it, and the only question is how much effort you'll spend finding them.


Next, let the deadline decide between the options that are left. A listing can take a week to find the right buyer, and a charity pickup or city collection runs on someone else's calendar. If the new sofa is being delivered Saturday morning and the old one has to be out by Friday night, the routes that wait on another person drop away and a haul you schedule yourself is what's left.


Finally, work out the carry and transportation. A free couch on the fourth floor of a walk-up attracts plenty of messages and very few people who turn up with a friend and a strap. If you can't get the piece to the curb or into a vehicle yourself, plan for help with both, whichever route it takes.


## How can you sell old furniture fast?


Sell old furniture faster by pricing it for its condition, photographing it in daylight, and including the measurements in the listing so nobody drives across town for a sofa that won't fit their door. Name the brand if there is one. A buyer searching for a West Elm sofa or an IKEA Hemnes dresser finds yours; a buyer searching for "dresser" scrolls past forty others.


The phrase that kills the most furniture sales is "pickup only." Plenty of buyers want the piece and have no way to move it, so a sale stalls at the moment they ask whether you deliver. Add a line to the Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist listing saying the buyer can book Lugg for pickup, and include your Lugg referral code so they get a discount on their first Lugg. The buyer books it, the movers collect from you, and the sale can close the same day. Settle payment with the buyer before the movers arrive, because Luggers can't pay a seller on the buyer's behalf.


## How can you get rid of furniture for free?


To get rid of usable furniture for free, list it in a local Buy Nothing group, Craigslist, or Facebook Marketplace and require pickup. A decent bookshelf can find a taker within a day or two. Give a pickup window so the conversation doesn't drag on for a week.


For pieces nobody will take, your city's bulk pickup is the free route, and the rules are set locally. In New York City, residents[get free curbside removal of furniture that's too big for a bin or bag](https://www.nyc.gov/site/dsny/collection/get-rid-of/furniture-mattresses.page) , the city asks you to take items apart where possible before setting them out, and mattresses and box springs have to be sealed in plastic bags. Other cities collect on a fixed day, ask you to book an appointment, or charge per item, so check your city's sanitation page before anything goes to the curb. Renters can also ask the building: some landlords run a bulk dumpster or a scheduled haul around move-out season.


## Should you donate old furniture?


Donating is worth it for furniture that's clean, complete and working, and it's the route that keeps a good piece in use. Each donation center sets its own standards and can turn a piece down on arrival, and individual locations set their own rules too, so call the one you're planning to use before you book anything. If you itemize, keep the charity's receipt and a record of the furniture's fair market value;[IRS documentation rules](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p526) depend on the amount you claim.


Free charity pickups exist, and they run on the charity's schedule and coverage area, which may or may not match your deadline. Dropping the piece off yourself is faster when it fits in your car. When it doesn't,[furniture donation pickup](https://lugg.com/furniture-donation-pickup) through Lugg covers the gap: movers load it at your place and unload it at the donation center you picked, on the day you need it gone.


## How do you dispose of furniture nobody wants?


Dispose of furniture nobody wants at a landfill, transfer station, or recycling center that accepts the item. It'll have plenty of company there. Americans generated[12.1 million tons of furniture and furnishings waste in 2018, and 80.1% of it was landfilled](https://www.epa.gov/facts-and-figures-about-materials-waste-and-recycling/durable-goods-product-specific-data) , according to the EPA. Some facilities recycle metal frames and mattresses separately, which makes it worth a call before you assume everything goes in the same pile.


Before you go, check three things with the facility: its hours, its fees, and whether it takes the specific item. Our guide on[how to find a dump or donation center near you](https://lugg.com/blog/how-to-find-a-dump-or-donation-center) walks through finding one. If you don't have a truck, Lugg's[junk removal](https://lugg.com/junk-removal) is the transport half of the job: Lugg movers load the furniture and drive it to the facility you choose, and you pick that facility and check its rules first.


This is also where splitting a load pays off. One Lugg can make up to five stops, so the bookshelf can go to a donation center and the broken futon to the dump on the same trip.


## How can you get heavy furniture out of the house?


To get heavy furniture out safely, choose its destination, measure the exit route, remove detachable parts, and clear the path before lifting.


### 1: Choose a destination for the old furniture


Know the destination first, whether that's a buyer's address, a donation center or a transfer station. A piece that leaves the room with nowhere to go ends up in a hallway or a garage for another month.


### 2: Measure the furniture and the exit route


Measure the piece's height, width and depth, then the narrowest doorway, stairwell turn and elevator door between it and the street. If the numbers are close, plan to take it apart or tip it on its end.


### 3: Remove drawers, cushions, legs, and shelves


Pull drawers, remove cushions, unscrew legs and lift out shelves. Put the screws and bolts in a labeled bag taped to the frame, because a buyer or donation center will want a complete piece.


### 4: Clear the furniture's path and protect the floors


Clear the hallway and stairs, prop open the doors and lay down something under the path if the floors scratch easily. Empty every drawer and cabinet, since anything left inside shifts and adds weight on the stairs.


### 5: Book movers for furniture you can't carry safely


A sleeper sofa, a solid wood armoire or a dresser on the third floor is a job for more than one pair of hands. Lugg handles items up to 250 lbs on any vehicle that comes with two Luggers (Pickup, Van, XL, Box or Box+), and up to 125 lbs on a Lite, which comes with one. You choose the vehicle when you book: a Pickup for one or two large pieces, a Van for a few pieces that need to stay dry, and an XL or a Box for a full load of large furniture. When in doubt, size up.


Mattresses come with their own rules, like New York's plastic-bag requirement, and our guide on[how to get rid of a mattress](https://lugg.com/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-a-mattress) covers them.


## How can you get old furniture out before the new piece arrives?


If you'd rather not carry the old piece out yourself, book[furniture removal](https://lugg.com/furniture-removal) through Lugg. Enter both addresses to see an upfront estimate, and one Lugg can drop the sofa at a donation center and the broken bed frame at the dump on the same trip.
